_note: WhatsDaf's own English renderings of the Hebrew commentaries on Sefaria (Vilna edition). Keys are <commentary>:<amud><segment>.<comment>. Square brackets are our clarifications. Very long Tosafot are condensed and marked "In brief".
rashi:a1.1: To establish them: as suspects. Did Rabbi Meir say “one suspected of one matter is suspected of the entire Torah” [about them]? [He said it only] where it is established for us that a person transgresses one matter.
tosafot:a1.1: Granted that Rabbi Meir said this with regard to a concern, etc.: From the wording it appears that this is said according to Rabbi Meir, and we do not hold like him; rather, even one established as transgressing one matter is not suspected regarding the entire Torah. And although in the chapter Zeh Borer (Sanhedrin 27a) Abaye said that a transgressor who eats carcasses provocatively is disqualified from testimony, and it is established according to Rabbi Meir, and we hold like him, since it is one of [the six rulings where the halakha follows Abaye, mnemonic] Ya’al Kagam, that is specifically with regard to testimony, for the Merciful One said: “Do not put your hand with the wicked to be an unrighteous witness”; but in other matters he is not suspected. However, Rabbi Meir, who says there that a conspiring witness is disqualified for the entire Torah, could equally have mentioned any of the other matters; he mentioned a conspiring witness only to exclude the view of Rabbi Yosei, who validates even a conspiring witness for capital cases when he was found conspiring in monetary cases.
gershom:a1.1: Granted that Rabbi Meir said “one suspected about a matter” with regard to a mere concern, where perhaps he is suspected; to establish them as certainly suspected he did not say [it]. Therefore they are not suspected regarding the entire Torah, and they are fit to judge.
rashi:a2.1: For testimony about a firstborn: to testify that he did not inflict this blemish deliberately.
rashi:a3.1: For the testimony of a woman: [testimony] that her husband died overseas.
rashi:a3.2: Teach: only for testimony for which a woman is valid: and in testimony about a firstborn a woman is also valid, since we say that the halakha follows Rabban Shimon [ben Gamliel], and even his daughter [may testify].
gershom:a2.1: For testimony for which a woman is valid. And a woman is valid for testimony about a firstborn, since we say: even his son, even his daughter.
rashi:a4.1: Yeimar permits firstborns: “Yeimar, the one who permits firstborns”, a derogatory expression.
rashi:a5.1: They were not established: that it is a firstborn, and the priest, its owner, came and said: This is a firstborn and its blemish is with it, meaning this blemish was not inflicted deliberately; and he came to show it to a Sage [to find out] whether it is permanent or passing.
rashi:a5.2: He is deemed credible: for the mouth that prohibited, by saying “it is a firstborn”, is the mouth that permitted, by saying “its blemish is with it”.
rashi:a6.1: I was a married woman: and we had never established that she was a married woman.
rashi:a6.2: She is deemed credible: and she is permitted to marry.
rashi:a7.1: For if she wanted she would not have said it: that is, if she were suspected of marrying during her husband’s lifetime without a divorce, she would have kept silent and not said “I was a married woman”, for we presume her to be unmarried.
rashi:a7.2: But here: with a firstborn, where he cannot avoid saying “it is a firstborn”, so that the Sage will tell him whether it is a permanent or a passing blemish. For with unblemished consecrated animals the priest is not suspected of eating them outside [the Temple], as that is a matter of karet; but he is suspected of inflicting a blemish on it, which is a mere prohibition. So [one might think] he should not be credible. [Rabbi Ile’a] teaches us that he is credible.
rashi:a8.1: For if so: if he had inflicted a blemish on it, he would have inflicted a blemish recognizable as a blemish even to an ignoramus, and he would no longer need to come before us and say “it is a firstborn”, for no one else knows that it is a firstborn; and as for consecrated meat outside [the Temple], he would have no doubt either, since he inflicted an obvious blemish on it. But where we know that it is a firstborn, one cannot say this, for he is forced to come before us: if he slaughtered it without an expert, since everyone knows that it is a firstborn, they would suspect him.
gershom:a3.1: Lest you say it is there: with a woman we say “the mouth that prohibited is the mouth that permitted”, for if she wanted she would say nothing, and we would not presume her to be a married woman, as no one knows.
gershom:a4.1: But here: with a firstborn, he cannot avoid saying [it is a firstborn] and having [the expert] testify, since he knows that it is a firstborn, and he will not eat consecrated meat outside [the Temple] unless [the expert] testifies about it that it is a blemish; so let us not say “the mouth that prohibited is the mouth that permitted”. [Rabbi Ile’a] teaches us that we do say it: since he could have inflicted on it an obvious blemish, which is certainly permanent, and he did not, we say “the mouth that prohibited is the mouth that permitted”.
tosafot:a10.1: And Rava said: why would he lie: We read “Rabba”, who was Abaye’s teacher, and not “Rava”. For Rava explicitly holds in [the chapter] Ḥezkat HaBatim (Bava Batra 33b) that we do not say “why would he lie” where there are witnesses, since it says there that Abaye and Rava do not accept that [ruling] of Rav Ḥisda, etc.
rashi:a10.1: In a place of witnesses: for we are witnesses that there is water there at all times. So too here, since we are witnesses that priests are suspected about blemishes, let us not say “why would he lie”.
rashi:a11.1: Here, did he certainly inflict a blemish on it? Said in astonishment.
gershom:a5.1: We do not say “why would he lie” in a place of witnesses: for we are witnesses that on the road of Nehar Pekod there is always water. So too here, since we know that priests are suspected about blemishes, let us not say “the mouth that prohibited is the mouth that permitted”. Here, with this priest who came and said “it is a firstborn and its blemish is with it”, do we know for certain that he inflicted a blemish on it? It is a mere concern, and in a place of concern we say “the mouth that prohibited is the mouth that permitted”.
rashi:a11.3: Without [naming] the man: he stated it anonymously: “If they had not established that it is a firstborn,” etc.
gershom:a6.1: Wicker baskets [natzrin hutzin]: baskets of peeled willow, which are thin and sharp. [Rabbeinu Gershom’s wording; our text of the Gemara has simply “baskets”.]
rashi:a12.1: Did we differentiate between a priest who is a ḥaver and a priest who is an ignoramus: and am I suspected of deliberately inflicting a blemish on it, like an ignorant priest?
gershom:a7.1: Did we differentiate between a ḥaver and an ignoramus: that although an ignoramus is suspected of causing a blemish in a firstborn, as it says, “if its owners are with us they may testify, and if not, not,” a priest who is a ḥaver is not suspected, and [since the blemish happened] without his intent, I could testify about it; or not? Rabbi Yehoshua said to him: Yes.
rashi:a12.2: Yes: we differentiated, and you are not suspected.
tosafot:a13.1: He came before Rabban Gamliel; he said to him: No: And this is the halakha, that there is no distinction between a ḥaver and an ignoramus. For in the last chapter of Yoma (78a), regarding Rabbi Yosei ben Zimra, who was a priest, it was asked whether the halakha follows Rabbi Meir, who says one suspected about a matter may neither judge it nor testify about it, or Rabban Shimon ben Gamliel, who says he is credible about his fellow’s. Learn from this that according to Rabbi Meir he would not permit [it], even though he was a ḥaver.
rashi:a13.1: Masters of the shields: shield-bearers; Torah scholars who fight in the war of Torah.
tosafot:a14.1: The questioner stood and asked: In the chapter Na’ara [HaMeorasa] of Nedarim, the Jerusalem Talmud derives from “And the two men shall stand,” [written] with the vav, that one who asks about halakhot and aggadot must stand.
gershom:a10.1: Rabbi Yehoshua said to him: No: because he did not want to issue a halakhic ruling in the presence of Rabban Gamliel.
tosafot:a15.1: Stand on your feet and they will testify against you: We do not read “and they will testify against you”, neither here nor at the beginning of the chapter Tefillat HaShaḥar (Berakhot 27b), for what testimony is relevant here? Rather, it is read in Sanhedrin, at the beginning of the chapter Kohen Gadol (Sanhedrin 19a), in the incident of Yannai, and from familiarity with the wording there it was written here.
rashi:a15.1: How shall I act: [i.e., how] can I contradict him?
rashi:a15.2: If I were alive and he were dead: I could contradict him and say, “I did not say it.”
rashi:a15.3: How can the living contradict the living: certainly I said so, and I retract.
tosafot:a15.2: How can the living contradict the living: That is, I thought to conceal it, but I cannot. And the Kuntres [Rashi] explained: certainly I said so, and I retract. But it cannot be so, for in the chapter Tefillat HaShaḥar (Berakhot 27b) the halakha is ruled there in accordance with him [Rabbi Yehoshua].
gershom:a12.1: And this is what it says in Berakhot: “He distressed him [also] in [the matter of] firstborns.”
rashi:a16.1: Stop, and he stopped: be silent, and he was silent.
tosafot:a16.1: Rabbi Ḥutzpit the disseminator: one of the ten martyrs executed by the [Roman] government.
rashi:a17.1: Mishna. I showed this firstborn: to a Sage, and he told me that it is a permanent blemish; and he may slaughter it, provided he has witnesses that he did not inflict it on it.
rashi:a18.1: Gemara. A priest is deemed credible to say: to a Sage, “An Israelite gave [me] this firstborn with this blemish that is on it.”
rashi:a18.2: That is likely to be revealed: for the Sage may come and say, “I did not permit it to you.”
gershom:a13.1: That is likely to be revealed: for one can ask the Sage whether he permitted it to him or not.
rashi:a19.1: No; actually I can tell you that about a matter likely to be revealed people do lie. And here, this is the reason he is credible: priests are not suspected of eating unblemished consecrated animals outside [the Temple]. Therefore, if the Sage had not permitted it to him, he would not say “he permitted it to me” and slaughter it without an expert’s permission.
gershom:a14.1: It is there: since he slaughtered it and says, “I showed it to a Sage and it is blemished,” he is credible. For since he is eating it, he surely knows that he may not eat consecrated meat outside [the Temple], and he certainly showed it.
rashi:a19.2: But here: where he shows it to the Sage and says, “An Israelite gave it to me with [this] blemish,” so that he will not need to bring witnesses that it fell on it by itself. Since priests are suspected of inflicting a blemish and saying it fell by itself, they are also suspected of inflicting a blemish and saying, “An Israelite gave it to me with its blemish.”
gershom:a15.1: But here: with a priest who said, “An Israelite gave me this firstborn with its blemish,” since it is alive and he has not slaughtered it, he is not credible, and we do not permit him to slaughter it, for they are suspected; perhaps he inflicted a blemish on it. And Rav Yehuda’s [reason], that it is likely to be revealed because one can ask [the Israelite] whether he sold it to him, does not hold.
rashi:a20.1: Buy for me from one who is trusted: who does not buy produce from an ignoramus; or from one who buys from an ignoramus and tithes the demai before selling it.
rashi:a20.2: Is not [credible]: this agent is [not] credible to say, “I bought it from a trusted person.”
rashi:b1.1: As he has [a way] of extricating himself: by saying, “If to you he is not trustworthy, I considered him trustworthy.” Therefore he is not afraid from the outset.
gershom:b1.1: It is different there, as the agent can extricate himself: for he can say, “I did not buy it from this one but from another, even from an ignoramus,” since he can say, “Even an ignoramus is trustworthy to me to buy from him.” Therefore the agent is not credible.
rashi:b2.1: From so-and-so: since the sender mentioned to him the name of the trusted person, this agent is credible, for he worries, “Perhaps he will question me and I will be found lying.” And this latter clause certainly supports Rav Yehuda, that people do not lie about a matter that is likely to be revealed.
gershom:b2.1: The latter clause supports Rav Yehuda. Where he said to him, “Buy for me from so-and-so, who is trusted,” this agent is credible to say that he bought from him, for now he cannot extricate himself.
rashi:b3.1: There, since there is a claimant, he is afraid: that is, do not support him from this. For there the agent is afraid: since he sees that the sender took care to mention the man’s name, he thinks he will certainly question him. But with the firstborn, this priest is not afraid, for he thinks: who will bother to look into my words and ask that Israelite whether he gave it to me with its blemish?
gershom:b3.1: But it is not so: there is no support for him from this. There, [regarding] “from so-and-so, who is trusted,” the agent is [certainly credible], for since he has a claimant, as the sender will ask that trusted so-and-so whether his agent bought from him, the agent is afraid and buys only from that one.
gershom:b4.1: But a priest who said, “An Israelite gave me this firstborn with its blemish,” has no claimant: no one bothers to ask the Israelite whether he gave it to him with its blemish. Therefore it does not support him.
rashi:b4.1: From where does Yehuda [know] this: what we said above: a priest is credible to say, “An Israelite gave me this firstborn with its blemish.”
rashi:b4.2: I fixed it with Giddul: I taught it to Giddul, and he taught it to Rav Yehuda; and this is what I said to Giddul: an Israelite is credible to say, etc. Another version: “I fixed it with a great one [gadol]”: I taught it to one great Sage.
gershom:b5.1: This: I fixed it with Giddul. That is, I taught it to Giddul, and Giddul taught it to Rav Yehuda.
gershom:b6.1: An Israelite? That is obvious: for they are not suspected about blemishes.
rashi:b5.1: With a young one: the lamb was small when he gave it to him.
rashi:b5.2: Lest you say he is not sure of it: because the lamb has grown, he does not recognize it, and perhaps it is another one, and this priest inflicted a blemish on it.
gershom:b7.1: No, it is necessary in the case of a minor who grew up: that is, that Israelite was a minor when he gave this firstborn with its blemish to the priest, and now, when he is an adult, he testifies about it that it is the same blemish that was on it when he gave it to him. [Rabbeinu Gershom reads “a young one” as the Israelite, not the animal; Rashi and the Davidson English read it as the animal.]
gershom:b8.1: Lest you say he is not sure of it [a note in the printed text corrects the wording to “lo kim leih beih”]: whether this is the very blemish that was on it when he gave it to him, because he was a minor and does not remember. [Rabbi Yirmeya bar Abba] teaches us that he is credible.
rashi:b6.1: In accordance with the latter version: an Israelite is credible.
rashi:b6.2: In accordance with the first version: that even the priest is credible. And the halakha is even in accordance with the first version.
tosafot:b6.1: And the halakha is even in accordance with the first version: And even though here we rule that people do not lie about a matter likely to be revealed, nevertheless [in the case of a woman whose husband is reported dead] one witness is believed only because she investigates carefully and [only then] marries. Alternatively, [both reasons are needed because] perhaps, since she loves him, she would not investigate carefully. And according to the one who says here that [the priest] is not credible even about a matter likely to be revealed, one can distinguish between this priest and a [single] witness. Alternatively, with regard to a woman they were lenient because of [her becoming] an aguna, and also because she investigates carefully.
gershom:b9.1: [Another version: the lamb was young.] And the halakha follows the first version, for about any matter likely to be revealed people do not lie.
rashi:b7.1: One day he was ill: Rafram, in his eyes.
rashi:b7.2: He brought it: this priest brought the firstborn before him to see whether it is a permanent blemish. And that priest thought: now his eyes hurt, and he will not recognize that this is the one he gave me without a blemish.
gershom:b11.1: He brought it before him: that very firstborn that he had given him, for he thought: now that his eyes hurt, he will not recognize it.
rashi:b7.3: He forced his eyes open: he opened his eye with force.
rashi:b7.4: He saw it and recognized it [bashkerei]: he recognized that he had given it to him without a blemish.
tosafot:b7.1: He saw it and recognized it [bashkerei]: This means he saw it and recognized it, for bashkerei is an expression of recognition, as in “one who has relations with a gentile woman, his foreskin is drawn and [Abraham] does not recognize him [mivashker leih]” in the chapter Osin Pasin (Eruvin 19a), and as in “he passed before them and they did not recognize him [bashkerei]” in the last chapter of Yevamot (120a). And the Kuntres [Rashi] did not explain it so.
gershom:b12.1: He forced his eyes open: that is, Rafram opened his eyes wide.
rashi:b8.1: He was unconcerned: Rafram, about the matter, [that is, he did not] say that a priest should no longer be credible to say, “An Israelite gave me this firstborn with its blemish.”
rashi:b8.2: It is this one who is impudent: for he showed himself impudent in two respects: first, that he inflicted a blemish on it; and further, that he should have shown it to another Sage, and he showed it to the very one who gave it to him.
gershom:b13.1: And even so he was unconcerned by the matter: [that is, he did not] decree that no priest who says, “An Israelite gave me this firstborn with its blemish,” should be believed; rather, he is credible. For he held: it is this one who is impudent, who did this.
rashi:b9.1: Sarua: one of its eyes large and one small.
rashi:b9.2: Whether it is a priest, whether it is an Israelite: for he did not know whether this was a priest or an Israelite, and he said: even if he is a priest and suspected about the firstborn, there is no suspicion here, for it was born this way.
gershom:b14.1: What should we be concerned about? This blemish is certainly by the hand of Heaven. Whether it is a priest or an Israelite who brought it, certainly its blemish is with it, and it is permitted.
rashi:b10.1: Unless a priest is with him: for perhaps, if [the expert] tells him it is permanent, he will slaughter it and eat it [himself]. For since it is permanent it may be eaten by anyone, except that it is the stolen property of a priest, and this one is not concerned about theft and eats it.
gershom:b15.1: But perhaps it is an Israelite who came, and one does not examine a firstborn for an Israelite unless a priest is with him, for we suspect that perhaps, after we permit it to him, he will not give it to the priest but will eat it himself. Therefore we require a priest with him, so that he will give it to him immediately. So why do you permit it, if it is an Israelite’s?
rashi:b11.1: How can these be compared? There: with other blemishes, which are not clear-cut, there is reason to suspect the Israelite that he may rob the priest. And even though he is a proper person in this matter, in that he wants to slaughter it only on the basis of an expert, granted that he will not eat consecrated meat outside [the Temple], for one who slaughters consecrated animals outside is [liable to] karet; nevertheless, about robbing a priest, which is a mere prohibition, he is suspected.
gershom:b16.1: How can these be compared? There, with a doubtful blemish, one does not examine it unless a priest is with him for this reason: granted that with an unblemished firstborn the Israelite is strict, for he will not eat consecrated meat outside [the Temple], but regarding the priest’s property, a blemished animal that has no sanctity, he is suspected of eating it. That is why one does not examine unless a priest is with him. But here, with this sarua, the Israelite surely knows that it is a clear-cut blemish, and since he did not neglect the honor of the Sage, he certainly will not commit a transgression, that we should suspect him of it.
tosafot:b12.1: Out of respect for the Sage: as it says below, three may permit a firstborn where there is no expert, and where there is an expert, not. Ruling: but this is obvious, that without permission it may not be slaughtered even if it has a clear-cut blemish, except on the basis of three or of an expert.
rashi:b12.1: He would commit a transgression? Said in astonishment: certainly he will not rob.
tosafot:b12.2: He does not neglect the respect due a Sage; would he commit a transgression: And if you say: for this reason, all firstborns with a clear-cut blemish that priests bring before us should be permitted without testimony! One can say: a priest is different, for he is afraid to eat it without a Sage’s permission, lest through this the matter be revealed that he inflicted a blemish on it. But of this Israelite one cannot say that he brings it before a Sage lest it become known that he wants to eat it and rob the priest of it, for even now, by doing this, it will not be made clear that he will not eat it himself.
rashi:b13.1: Mishna. Everyone is credible about the blemishes of a tithe: to testify that it fell on it by itself. And it is speaking of a doubtful tithe, for example where he called the ninth “tenth”, about which we say in the last chapter (below, Bekhorot 59a) that it is not eaten and has no remedy except through a blemish.
rashi:b14.1: Gemara. Does he know which will emerge: at the opening, as tenth, that he could inflict a blemish on it from the outset?
rashi:b15.1: At the head of ten: that is, as the tenth.
rashi:b16.1: Mishna. Whose eye was blinded: which is a clear-cut blemish.
rashi:b17.1: Gemara. Outside the Land: where it is not fit to be sacrificed, even in the time of the Temple, [as stated] in tractate Temura (21b).
tosafot:b17.1: The permitting of a firstborn outside the Land on the basis of three synagogue-goers: We would not learn this from our mishna, for it can be explained as referring to nowadays; but when the Temple stands one might have decreed [regarding] outside the Land on account of the Land of Israel, not to be lenient and permit [it] on the basis of three synagogue-goers. And further, because there is an opinion in Temura, chapter Elu Kodashim (Temura 21a), that firstborns from outside the Land, if they arrived unblemished, are sacrificed.
gershom:b17.1: What is he teaching us? We learn: a firstborn, etc. And the mishna is dealing with outside the Land and nowadays, since it teaches [elsewhere] “old, with its hair hanging down”; for if it entered your mind [that it speaks of] the time of the Temple, they should have sacrificed it [before it grew old].
gershom:b18.1: Three synagogue-goers: for we do not require full experts.
gershom:b19.1: And with clear-cut blemishes, which are recognizable, such as an eye blinded or [a leg] severed.
gershom:b20.1: To convey the strength of Rabbi Yosei: that even with clear-cut [blemishes] he says that it may be slaughtered only on the basis of an expert.
rashi:b20.1: Uncertain: uncertain whether he said it to me in the name of Rav, uncertain whether he said it to me in the name of Shmuel.
rashi:b20.2: Three may permit the firstborn, etc.: with clear-cut blemishes.
tosafot:b20.1: We learn: that animal may be slaughtered, etc.: Why does it not answer here that [Rav Yehuda’s ruling comes] to exclude the view of Rabbi Yosei, as is said shortly [of Rav Ḥiyya bar Amram], even though [Rabbi Yosei’s] reasoning is with him? Because if so, Rav Yehuda should have said “the halakha follows the Rabbis” or “the halakha does not follow Rabbi Yosei.” But Rabbi Ḥiyya [Rav Ḥiyya bar Amram] below mentioned two matters on one subject, permitting a firstborn and permitting vows.
tosafot:b21.1: Where there is an expert, not: Not specifically an expert whom the court has authorized. For of Rav Ashi above we said that they brought that sarua before him out of respect for the Sage; and anyone outstanding in wisdom and expert is fit to permit a firstborn or a vow alone, as is implied by [the incident of] Rav Ashi above. And in the first chapter of Nedarim (8b), regarding Ravina, who had a vow concerning his wife and came before Rav Ashi, etc., it says “learn from it three [things]”, etc., “and a single expert may release a ban”; this implies somewhat that a single expert is [someone] like Rav Ashi. And similarly that [statement] in the first chapter of Sanhedrin (5b), “but if he was an expert for the public, he may judge even alone,” does not mean specifically an ordained expert, etc., as Rav Naḥman said there: “For example, one like me may judge monetary cases [alone].” Ruling: However, nowadays it does not appear that any person is considered an expert to permit a firstborn or a vow alone, or to judge monetary cases [alone].
tosafot:b22.1: Three may dissolve a vow where there is no Sage: Compare in this matter the first chapter of Nedarim (8b), [where we say] a person may not dissolve a vow in the place of his teacher. However, there, even if another expert is present, that expert may not dissolve [it] in the place of his teacher, like Ravina in the place of Rav Ashi.
